title: Polymorphism
hook: virtual opens a dispatch slot. override replaces it. abstract demands a replacement. sealed override closes it. new hides a name and does not touch the slot — the bug that looks like polymorphism in a code review.

sections.heading: The dispatch slot
sections.prose: When you call handler.Parse(raw) through a base type, the CLR uses the method table of the runtime object if Parse is virtual and overridden. That is subtype polymorphism. Overload resolution is compile-time and is not polymorphism. Generic constraints (module 09) are another story. Keep virtual members small and documented; every virtual is a compatibility promise.

sections.heading: new hiding versus override
sections.prose: If the base method is not virtual, you cannot override it. Writing public new void Parse looks like a replacement but is a second method. Call sites typed as the base still invoke the base method. That is why interviewers paste a three-class sample and ask what prints. sealed override prevents a further derived type from overriding again. abstract methods are virtual with no body; the type must be abstract.

snippets.label: override versus new
snippets.explanation: Name is in the slot. Kind is a different member. The compile-time type decides which Kind you see.

sections.heading: Practical restraint
sections.prose: Template Method with a few protected abstract hooks is enough for an auth family. Deep virtual stacks in a high-concurrency submit path make reasoning and inlining harder. Prefer sealing workers. Interface polymorphism (next) is often the better seam because it does not consume your single base class.

interviewTakeaways: virtual/override is runtime dispatch; new is hiding.
You cannot override a non-virtual instance method.
sealed override stops the slot from opening again.
commonPitfalls: Calling virtual methods from constructors — derived override runs before derived initialization completes.
Using new by accident after a refactor that should have been override.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS ‘override’ is just assigning a function on the derived prototype. There is no virtual keyword; hiding versus override is not a language distinction.
TS override is a compile-time check that a base method exists. It does not create a CLR slot. C# override is metadata.
